sections.chief_complaint: Left knee pain, progressive worsening over the past 2 months.
sections.hpi: 46-year-old active female, 2-month history of worsening left knee pain. Morning stiffness, inability to perform a full squat, progressive functional limitation. Minor tweak while playing ball in the backyard with her children ~2 months ago, pain progressively worsened since. Remote left knee injury from skiing in her 20s, healed conservatively with immobilisation, no surgery, imaging obtained at the time (records unavailable). Denies significant knee problems between the old injury and now. Pain medial aspect of the left knee; aggravated by stairs (ascending and descending) and squatting; morning stiffness with a slight limp on waking that resolves; intermittent swelling with occasional change in the appearance of the knee; no other joint pain, right knee asymptomatic; managed with Tylenol and Advil PRN, no formal treatment. Highly active: swimming 3x/week, dancing, resistance work ~2x/week, limited by the knee pain.
sections.past_medical_history: Crohn's disease (stable). Perimenopausal, recently commenced HRT. Previous left knee injury (skiing, 20s), resolved conservatively. Back fracture at age 16 (motor vehicle accident), surgically reduced and repaired.
sections.past_surgical_history: 3x Caesarean sections. Abdominoplasty. Breast lift. Liposuction. Tonsillectomy. Reduction and scar repair of back fracture (age 16, MVA) under general anaesthesia, no complications. Dilatation and curettage. No prior anaesthetic complications.
sections.medications: Adalimumab (Humira) 40 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks. Semaglutide (Ozempic) 1 mg subcutaneous weekly. Estrogen gel (half dose, per patient report). Progesterone 1 tablet orally at night. Testosterone supplementation planned pending tolerance of current HRT. Tylenol / Advil PRN.
sections.physical_exam: General: well-appearing, well-groomed adult female, alert and conversational, no acute distress at rest. Both knees — Inspection: no gross deformity, no gross swelling. Milking test: no effusion seen. Range of motion: full passive ROM both knees, pain only on the left at maximal knee flexion. Palpation at ~90 degrees flexion at both medial and lateral joint lines: no pain on right; pain on left at medial posterior joint line only. Patellar mobility tested without pain; patellar grind test done, no pain either side. Ligament stability: ligaments clinically stable; Lachman manoeuvre done on both knees, negative. McMurray test done: negative on the right, positive on the left.
sections.imaging_review: Bilateral standing AP view: medial joint space narrowing (left knee), consistent with early degenerative changes; right side comparatively better preserved. Lateral projection of both knees: small osteophytes at proximal patellar pole on both sides, worst on left. Axial / sunrise (Merchant) view both knees: small osteophyte and mild arthritic change under the patella (patellofemoral compartment) on the left; right patellofemoral compartment appears well maintained.
sections.assessment: 46-year-old active female with left knee pain and functional limitation. Clinical and radiographic findings consistent with early degenerative joint disease in the medial compartment and patellofemoral joint of the left knee. A medial meniscal tear cannot be excluded and is to be further assessed on MRI. 1. Left knee medial compartment osteoarthritis (early) — radiographic joint space narrowing with degenerative changes. 2. Possible medial meniscal tear — cannot be excluded on X-ray; MRI indicated. 3. Patellofemoral osteoarthritis (left > right) — small osteophyte under patella on axial view. 4. Contributing factors: perimenopause, high activity level, prior knee injury.
sections.plan: Investigations: MRI left knee, prescription provided today, to assess cartilage integrity and meniscal status; MRI not required before proceeding with injection. Referrals: physiotherapy, prescription provided today, to strengthen muscles around the knee to offload the joint and optimise injection outcomes; patient counselled physiotherapy is essential regardless of injection choice. Injection options discussed, patient to decide and may return at a subsequent visit: (1) cortisone — basic pain relief, not considered beneficial for joint preservation; (2) viscosupplementation (hyaluronic acid) ~$450, joint lubricant, selected brand includes a corticosteroid component for initial inflammation, can be more painful to inject due to viscosity; (3) PRP ~$900, autologous blood drawn and centrifuged, platelet-rich fraction re-injected, natural anti-inflammatory, supports cartilage health.
